newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish government sells its budget to the left.
newsitem.headline: Danish government sells its budget to the left.

text.p: Denmark's minority government signed a tactical agreement on Thursday with a far-left party, aimed at securing the passage through parliament of the 1997 budget and fending off right-wing plans to force an election.

The agreement, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, meets Socialist Peoples' Party (SPP) demands to fund adult education, training for the unemployed, social, environmental and cultural projects and improved conditions in the workplace.
In return, the SPP -- with a pivotal 13 seats in the 179-member parliament -- supports the government's bill for a balanced public sector budget.
"I am happy both with the content of the agreement and the responsible manner in which it was negotiated," Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft told Danish Radio.
Financial markets and analysts welcomed the deal, saying that the political stability it promised outweighed concerns about increased left-wing influence on the government.

The ruling coalition, vulnerable with only 76 seats to the right-wing opposition's combined 83, began wooing the left after budget talks with the Conservatives collapsed on November 1 over government plans to balance the budget through higher taxes.

A 0.1 percent rise in gross income tax was passed with leftist support last week. Thursday's agreement finances the SPP demands and the eradication of the forecast 5.8 billion Danish crown ($985.7 million) budget deficit largely by one-off measures.

One, which has shipowners howling with rage, is the liquidation of a state insurance fund against marine war damages estimated to contain some 3.5 billion crowns, built up from premiums from shipowners.
"As if by magic we have lost billions which we believe is morally our money," Uffe Lind Rasmussen of the Danish Shipowners' Association told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
Other funding is to come from the sale of state property holdings and the transfer of money from a workers' holiday fund.
The success of the deal rests on the tacit support of the radical, anti-establishment Unity List, which has six parliamentary seats.
The party is expected to abstain when the budget comes to parliament although a final decision will be taken at the weekend by its young and volatile 21-member central committee.
"That's the joker in the pack," a Conservative member of parliament told Reuters.

"The six members who sit in the house every day and have working experience of politics would not bring down the government and force an election liable to bring us into power but the committee just might, and the MPs must obey its orders."
A Unity List decision to vote against the finance bill would trigger an onslaught by the right, which has long been waiting for a chance to pounce on the unpopular government.

"We have said all along that if we have an opportunity to throw out this government we shall take it. If the Unity List is to vote against the budget then so shall we," Conservative Party spokeswoman Anne Birgite Lundholdt said on Tuesday.

Latest polls show the right winning an election if one were to be held now, with the Centre Democrats -- junior partners in the Social Democrat-led coalition -- failing to reach the threshold for a seat in parliament. ($1=5.884 Danish Crown)
